books.title: ASML's Architects
books.fullTitle: ASML's Architects: The Story of the Engineers Who Shaped the World's Most Powerful Chip Machines
books.author: René Raaijmakers
books.case: Best fit in this set: the conversion of difficult physics and engineering into a viable industrial system. The main chronology reaches 1996; this is an account of ASML's origins, not a full history of its later EUV business.
books.gate: Passes both hard exclusions. The author calls this the technical version, but explicitly distinguishes its popular historical treatment from specialist technical depth. Its chronological chapters concern people, machines, firms and commercial survival. Technical explanation supports the history; teaching lithography design or machine operation is not its main purpose. The SPIE catalogue label 'monograph' does not determine the classification.
books.veto: V1: interview memory and retrospective success attribution are limits, but no central factual or causal failure was established. V2: the author's enthusiasm and Dutch perspective require scrutiny; his stated search for dissenting accounts and inclusion of failure weigh against a finding of evidence-subordinating allegiance. V3: engineering coordination and commercialization provide transferable content. V4: the historical value survives changes in ASML's market position. No veto established.
books.theme: No deduction. This is a company and technology history with international suppliers, customers and competitors. Its Dutch base does not make its main subject single-nation history.
books.edition: First published in Dutch as De architecten van ASML in 2017. The author announced the English translation on 26 November 2018; some catalogues and the English copyright use 2019. Use 2017 for the original work, 2018 for first English availability, and distinguish later editions. The verified English print ISBN is hardcover, 664 pages. No English paperback ISBN was established.
reasons: Extensive access and interviews support the history; retrospective testimony and uneven coverage of foreign rivals limit causal certainty.
The account connects engineering choices with the constraints of building a reliable, saleable machine.
Supplier dependence, team coordination and the transition from research to production offer strong lessons for other complex technologies.
Technical development, organization, funding and market competition form a closely connected account.
The technical detail earns much of the length, but the large cast and local episodes increase reading cost.
The historical lessons do not depend on current chip-market publicity or forecasts.
An unusually direct match for physics, advanced machinery and industrial capability.
A long-standing technology journalist with strong access; less independent scholarly testing than a mature academic history.
The chronology is clear, but many participants make it demanding to follow.
Technical distinctions are treated seriously; this assessment rests on the available samples and evidence, not a full prose audit.

books.title: Never at Rest
books.fullTitle: Never at Rest: A Biography of Isaac Newton
books.author: Richard S. Westfall
books.case: The strongest choice here for the history of scientific reasoning and research conduct. Its main cost is the length: over 900 pages, including substantial personal, religious and institutional detail.
books.gate: Passes both hard exclusions on purpose and structure. This is a sustained scientific biography, organized around Newton's life and work, rather than a course, procedure manual or specialist mathematical reference. MAA classifies it as General and distinguishes its biographical aim from a technical presentation. Its inclusion as a profile example and its V3 science-biography exception are not substitutes for this check.
books.veto: V1: MAA identifies a problem in distinguishing Wallis's indivisibles from Newton's infinitesimals. This reduces evidence precision, but does not establish a failure of the biography's central account. V2: no serious evidence-subordinating allegiance established. V3: scientific practice, publication and institutional conflict provide content; the explicit science-biography exception also applies. V4: the historical value is durable. Newton's religious and alchemical beliefs are subjects of history, not supernatural claims endorsed as fact by this assessment. No veto established.
books.theme: No deduction. The main subject is Newton's scientific and intellectual life, not English national history, a political celebrity, or religious advocacy. Royal Mint and parliamentary episodes do not predominate.
books.edition: Use 1980 as the original year, supported by the Oxford Newton Project bibliography and library records. Cambridge Core calls it a 1981 biography and lists 31 January 1981, so the 1980/1981 metadata conflict is recorded rather than silently discarded. The linked complete paperback is ISBN 9780521274357, listed by MAA as 1983 and 928 pages; it is not the later shortened biography.
reasons: Deep archival scholarship supports the account; identified mathematical distinctions and interpretive reconstruction prevent full marks.
Shows the development of problems, evidence and concepts, though it is not a modern reconstruction of every derivation.
Useful for research habits, priority disputes and scientific institutions; fewer direct lessons for industry or strategic decisions.
Connects scientific work with intellectual commitments, correspondence, institutions and public duties.
The detail is valuable for sustained study but costly for this reader's preference for dense, reusable insight.
Foundational scientific history retains value even as later scholarship revises individual interpretations.
Directly addresses physics, mathematics and the organization of science without relying on elementary popular-physics exposition.
Westfall's specialist scholarship and the book's sustained critical reception support the strongest authority allocation.
The life provides a clear structure, but exhaustive detail slows the argument.
Controlled historical exposition; the specific mathematical weakness is charged principally to evidence integrity.

books.title: X, Y & Z
books.fullTitle: X, Y & Z: The Real Story of How Enigma Was Broken
books.author: Dermot Turing
books.case: A compact case of mathematical capability gaining strategic value through intelligence sharing and international cooperation. The institutional story is stronger than the technical explanation of cryptanalysis.
books.gate: Passes both hard exclusions. The publisher and specialist review identify a general-reader history of people and cooperation, not training in codebreaking. Incidental technical explanation does not change that purpose. The author is Dermot, not Dermont, Turing.
books.veto: V1: Ralph Erskine reports a Playfair substitution/transposition error, imprecise archival references and an unconvincing reconstructed exchange, but calls his criticisms minor and confined to details. They do not invalidate the central cooperation account. V2: correcting the balance of national credit is not itself national allegiance; no serious asymmetric treatment was established. V3: complementary expertise and information exchange offer transferable lessons. V4: the historical value is independent of current controversy. No veto established.
books.theme: No deduction. The central account spans French, Polish and British intelligence and mathematics with wider military consequences. Its emphasis on Polish contributions does not make it general single-nation history.
books.edition: Original publication 2018. The History Press lists the paperback on 14 May 2021, ISBN 9780750993937. Arkady Rzegocki wrote the foreword and is not a coauthor. The 2019 date in some hardcover records is not the original year.
reasons: Research across several archives supports the account; the documented errors and vague references prevent a higher evidence score.
Explains how institutions and complementary skills enabled progress, with less depth on the mathematics itself.
Strong lessons in sharing scarce knowledge, preserving expertise and coordinating under threat.
Connects mathematics, intelligence services, secrecy and wartime strategy, with limited treatment of wider production or finance.
About 320 pages is a reasonable scale; escape and personal-history passages add less reusable explanation.
The record of technical cooperation and secrecy has lasting value.
A close match for mathematics, computing history and military intelligence.
Archival work and favorable specialist scrutiny support authority; the family name alone earns no points.
The participants and wartime sequence provide a clear narrative frame.
Technical terminology and reconstructed dialogue show lapses in precision.

books.title: Why the West Rules—for Now
books.fullTitle: Why the West Rules—for Now: The Patterns of History, and What They Reveal About the Future
books.author: Ian Morris
books.case: The widest thematic match, but the weakest recommendation of these four. Its broad comparison can generate useful questions; the numerical index and long-range forecasts do not merit the trust one would place in a validated causal model.
books.gate: Passes both hard exclusions. The nominated book is comparative explanatory history for general readers. Its separate technical appendix is supporting evidence, not another nominated book, and does not turn the main narrative into specialist training.
books.veto: V1 is a close call. Kenneth Pomeranz argues that energy use dominates the preindustrial index, that regional units are problematic, and that measurement does not establish the proposed causal account. He nevertheless finds value in the narrative. Morris's response and methodological appendix openly discuss assumptions, error and ways to challenge the model. My judgment is that this establishes a contested and weakly validated synthesis, but not conclusively that its central geography–technology explanation depends on a material falsehood or invalid inference. The no-veto decision has LOW confidence; disclosure alone would not rescue a demonstrated central failure. V2: no evidence-subordinating allegiance established. V3: comparative mechanisms remain. V4: forecasts are vulnerable, but historical explanation supplies substantial independent value. Retain at a low priority rather than treating its model as settled knowledge.
books.theme: No deduction. This is comparative civilization and power history. Energy constraints, climate and disease enter parts of the explanation, but environmental issues or disease are not the predominant subject. Neither a single nation nor American domestic history organizes the book.
books.edition: First published in 2010. The verified Profile paperback is dated 4 August 2011, ISBN 9781846682087. The first year and purchase-edition year are kept separate.
reasons: Evidence and assumptions are exposed to criticism, but the validity of the aggregate measure remains disputed.
Offers causal hypotheses linking geography, technology and power; the index cannot by itself identify those effects.
Useful for framing comparative questions, less reliable for decisions that require specific estimates or forecasts.
Combines energy, organization, information, warfare and geography across a very large scope.
The synthesis earns much of its length; sweeping treatment sometimes replaces the detail needed to test a claim.
The historical comparisons endure, while the forecast section is less durable.
Directly addresses civilization, technological capacity and geopolitical power.
An established ancient historian with serious specialist engagement; authority does not settle modern global causal claims.
A clear comparative structure sustains a large argument.
The scale and numerical presentation can suggest greater precision than the evidence supports.
